title: Grimmir, the Old Man of the Forest
subtitle: Blood at Midwinter

lore.description:
Grimmir is the Old Man of the Forest, the Alder King, the presence that watches from the shadow of the oldest oak, the cold breath on the back of the neck when the path grows dark. He is not kind, nor is he cruel—he is wild, and the wild does not negotiate. It demands, and it takes. His followers learn to read the language of blood on snow, the geometry of root and stone, and the weight of a heart offered at the turning of the year. Grimmir does not teach harmony; he teaches respect through fear, and fear through sacrifice.

**The Thorn-Father at an inhabited boundary.**

Aelaerem do not cease to enjoy a hedgerow because it requires care. Berries are gathered, children know the sheltered places, and the person tying a red thread may also be the person who brought lunch. A Thorn-Father observance can be part of the same afternoon. When the necessary work becomes terrible, that household warmth need not turn out to have been false. Someone carries it through because a neighbor would otherwise have to.

Root-Moot practices passed between villages through seasonal work and marriage. A hedge laid by one family may preserve an observance their descendants no longer perform at home. Disputes concern which household will tend it and whose account of the last winter is trusted. They do not require a visiting priest to explain why the Alder King wants what he wants.

**The Root-Father below the tree line.**

Aeler Root-Father shrines attend fungus beds and stone-lichen as well as wooded slopes. A hold that reveres old growth below ground need not admit outsiders to its upper forest. In the Aelerian foothills, keepers have negotiated gathering rights with human households for generations; those agreements govern the people, not Grimmir. A paper allowing a tree to be cut does not make the grove approve.

The same devotion acquires a different scale in the Yundrath. A family's grove can lie below its dwelling across a gorge, and two relatives may reach it by different routes. When a bridge fails, the nearer human settlement can become responsible for work the hold previously insisted only its own keepers could perform. Gratitude and a quarrel about authority can arrive together.

**The wolf without a forest.**

Ykrul Sky-Wolf observances place seasonal movement where a forest village would place a boundary. The grass and the herds can be read without supposing a hidden oak behind every rite. Some camp keepers recognize Grimmir in the wolf that herds the seasons; others use the name only when speaking to outsiders and regard the comparison as incomplete.

Such identifications spread through shared winter camps and returned fosterlings. They need not demonstrate that one culture borrowed its entire religion from another. A keeper who learned a song among rivals may preserve it because it marked a season survived, while refusing to adopt the rivals' account of who first sang it.

**The old wood beside a new shrine.**

In Nihori, some forest shrines acknowledge Grimmir as the Elder at the Root. Their local kami remain local presences with their own standing. A grove can receive both observances without becoming an eastern province of the Alder King's Court. Processional visitors may leave an offering in a form the resident household finds unfamiliar but recognizes as careful.

The difficult history is often in an abandoned approach. A new road has made the old offering place inconvenient; a shrine household has served travelers for generations at the replacement. When the old growth begins intruding on the maintained road, no one needs to have lied. Decide what the grove requires and what can be learned before asking the party to intervene. The villagers' affection for their home and their fear of the wood should both survive the encounter.
lore.followers: Those who walk his path become keepers of the old ways: druids who know when a grove must be fed, rangers who leave the first kill for the soil, and hedge-folk who whisper the names of spirits not to be spoken aloud. Their magic is not the gentle coaxing of garden plants but the raw, patient hunger of the forest floor—a hunger that swallows bones and grows mushrooms in the shape of the dead.

names_across_regions.aeler: The Root-Father, a patron of deep fungus and stone-lichen whose shrines are carved into living rock
names_across_regions.ykrul: The Sky-Wolf, a spirit of the steppe who herds the seasons and grants omens
names_across_regions.aelaerem: The Thorn-Father, keeper of hedgerow magic, honored with red thread tied around roadside stones

lore.quote: The forest does not ask. It takes. The deer does not weep for the wolf, and the wolf does not beg the earth. Give what the season demands, or the season will take it anyway.

domain_focus: Seasonal Sacrifice: the old ways of blood and offering, the turning wheel that demands payment
Folk Horror: the terror of the unseen, the ritual that must be performed, the boundary that must not be crossed
Primal Mystery: knowledge hidden in root and stone, the language of omens and portents
Growth from Death: the forest floor as a stomach; decay as the engine of new life

thiasos.description: Grimmir's Thiasos is a small beast or mythological creature of the wild wood: a pine marten with eyes like amber, a raven that knows the migration routes of every bird, a fox with a single white paw that leaves no prints in snow, a toad that hibernates in rotten logs and sings at the first thaw, or a stag-calf with antlers budding like spring shoots.
thiasos.care: Beyond its ordinary care, this Thiasos must be allowed to roam freely in unspoiled nature each day. If confined for more than a day, it becomes Compromised (it scratches at doors, refuses to eat, and its coat grows dull; its bearer loses the benefit of Seasonal Sense until it is released).

codex.description: You will not find Grimmir's Codex bound as a book of paper and ink. It may be a slab of slate carved with seasonal runes that frost over in winter, a bundle of bark scrolls sealed with pine resin, a set of knotted cords woven from the hair of a wild boar, or the hollowed horn of a stag filled with charcoal and ash.
codex.upkeep: Because the wild resists being fixed in writing, the Codex requires upkeep: the Runekeeper must spend an hour each week in a natural place, re-carving or re-knotting the Rites by memory, or the symbols fade (treat as Compromised until restored under open sky).

patrons_gift.name: Grimmir's Blessing
patrons_gift.description: Once per scene as an action, a Runekeeper of Grimmir may touch a held item (weapon, tool, or garment) and whisper a word of the season.
patrons_gift.effect: For the rest of the scene, the item grants +1 die to Lore or Stealth rolls in natural terrain, and the first time each scene the bearer would be tracked by mundane means, the tracker suffers –1 die (the forest hides their trail).
patrons_gift.cost: After the scene, the user marks +1 Obligation to Grimmir.

rites.name: Rite of the Blood Offering
rites.materials: A drop of your own blood (1 Fatigue) or the blood of a freshly killed animal.
rites.effect: The forest accepts your offering. For the remainder of the scene, you gain +1 die to all Survival and Stealth rolls in natural terrain. Additionally, you may ask the GM one yes/no question about a threat hidden in the wilderness (e.g., 'Is there a predator watching us?').
rites.push_it: The offering is accepted with hunger—you gain +2 dice instead, but you must leave a visible token (a hair, a scrap of clothing) on the ground. That token can be used by the GM later as a sympathetic link (spend 1 SB to have an animal or spirit track you). Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Speaking Roots
rites.materials: Soil from a grave or a crossroads, held in the mouth.
rites.effect: You listen to the memory of the land. Gain +2 dice to Investigation or Lore when seeking to understand what happened in a natural place—a death, a ritual, a violation of the wild. The GM must give you a truthful but cryptic answer.
rites.push_it: The roots speak too clearly. You see a vision of the event, but it leaves you shaken: mark Fatigue 1 and the GM gains 1 SB. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Twisted Path
rites.materials: A knotted cord woven from thorns and hair.
rites.effect: The forest bends against your enemies. Choose a single target within Near. For the remainder of the scene, all their navigation, tracking, and movement rolls suffer –1 die as roots trip them, branches block their way, and the path turns subtly wrong.
rites.push_it: The curse also causes the target to suffer 1 Fatigue as they struggle against the hostile woods. Mark 1 SB (Diamonds) as the forest's malice becomes visible. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Heart's Meal
rites.materials: The fresh heart of an animal (or a sentient creature, if you dare), still warm.
rites.effect: You consume the heart raw. Gain one of the following: Heal 1 Harm (the heart's vitality transfers to you); Gain a +2 die bonus on your next physical action (the heart's strength); Learn a secret the creature knew in life (GM discretion; the heart whispers as you eat). After the rite, you are marked—animals within Near range are nervous around you (disadvantage on animal handling) for one scene.
rites.push_it: Eat the heart of a thinking creature. The benefit is doubled, but you gain a Hunger Condition (must eat another heart within a month or suffer 1 Fatigue per week). The GM gains 2 SB. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the World's Wound
rites.materials: A sacred grove-site, a circle of stones, an offering of blood or seed.
rites.effect: Heal a blighted place or quicken a damaged ecosystem. Clear taint, restore fertility, awaken dormant forces. Gain +2 dice to related Lore/Nature actions in the region. Start an Ecosystem Restoration [8] timer.
rites.push_it: The cure spreads to adjacent areas but unbalances another; mark 2 SB (Diamonds). Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +3) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Cycle's Crown
rites.materials: A circlet of woven branches, antlers, and seasonal tokens.
rites.effect: Become an avatar of the cycle. Choose two: Seasonal Mastery (+2 dice to all actions keyed to the current season: spring—healing and growth; summer—strength and harvest; autumn—preservation and preparation; winter—endurance and hiding); Verdant Command (command plant life in Near automatically); Cycle's Healing (remove one Condition or downgrade Harm by one level); Growth's Protection (allies gain +1 Armor from natural cover). Begin a Seasonal Avatar [6] timer.
rites.push_it: Extend the blessings to all present; mark +2 Obligation and gain Seasonal Attunement (see Corruption). Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +3) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

cantors.name: The Cantor's Song
cantors.description: A Cantor of Grimmir sings the drone of green things—a low, humming chant that mimics the vibration of leaves in wind or the deep thrum of growing roots. Their voice is used to coax reluctant seeds, to calm wounded animals, and to mark the turning of the seasons in rituals that entire villages attend. A Grimmir Cantor does not seek an audience; they sing to the land itself, and the land answers in fruit, rain, or silence.

cult.name: The Cult of the Root-Moot
cult.description: Grimmir's cults are neither secret nor organized—a 'moot' may be a single hermit or a scattered network of rangers who meet only at the solstices. The most ancient of these, the Root-Moot, carves masks from living moss and wears them during the rite of the Turning Wheel. Each member plants a tooth (their own or a beast's) into the root-ball of a sacred oak; if the tooth sprouts a sapling by spring, the planter is considered 'heard' by the Old Man. Their creed is carved into the oldest oak in each grove: 'Take only what the season gives. Give back what the season will need.' Outsiders are welcome at the solstice fires, but they must work—splitting wood, digging a drainage trench, or feeding the fire with a personal memory (which the flames accept with a green flash).

witchcraft.name: The Root and the Thorn
witchcraft.description: A witch who walks with Grimmir is a hedgewright or path-keeper—a crafter of living boundaries. Their work may be invisible: weaving a branch to guide deer away from a village, carving a marker that tells the frost when to end, or building a root bridge that only becomes passable at low tide. This craft can look like 'infrastructure'—an Aeler True-Mason might carve a stone that remembers the boundary between a mine and a sacred spring, or a Linn shipwright might season a keel with a prayer for the right wind. But the witch's tools are never hammers; they are twine, moss, and the quiet patience of waiting for the land to answer.
witchcraft.lore: The hedgewright's path is the oldest magic—older than temples, older than covenants. It is the memory of the land itself, shaped by patient hands and whispered prayers. To walk with Grimmir is to learn that the boundary is sacred, and that the wild must be respected, not tamed.
witchcraft.quote: The root does not bargain. It grows, or it rots.

hedge_gifts.name: Knot of the Turning Year
hedge_gifts.description: Once per scene, you may tie a simple knot (in a cord, a strand of hair, or a blade of grass) and speak a phrase appropriate to the current season. The knot subtly influences the weather or local plant growth for the next hour—a gust of wind, a sudden rain, or a patch of ivy that grows just enough to provide cover. The GM adjudicates effect.

hedge_gifts.name: Root-Reader
hedge_gifts.description: You may touch the exposed root of a tree and ask one yes/no question about the health of the land within a mile. The root pulses once for 'yes,' twice for 'no.' Once per scene.

hedge_gifts.name: Seasonal Barometer
hedge_gifts.description: You can predict the weather for the next 12 hours with 90% accuracy when in a natural setting. No roll required.

knotted_staff.name: The Knotted Staff
knotted_staff.description: A staff of petrified wood, cold to the touch but warm when it touches living matter. Once per session, when used to bless a boundary marker (a post, a stone, a tree), it inscribes a minor [SEASONAL] tag into the threshold. The marker will 'remember' the season of its carving for one year, granting +1 die to rolls that honor that season's work.

monastic_tradition.name: The Way of the Root and Stone
monastic_tradition.description: Monks of the Root and Stone tradition learn to move with the seasons and stand as immovable as the ancient oaks. They are guardians of the boundary between the civilized and the wild, and they know that the strongest defense is to be where the blow is not.
monastic_tradition.quote: The root does not break. It bends, and it waits. So too must you.

basic.name: Rooted Stance
basic.description: When you do not move during your turn, you gain +1 Armor until your next turn. The earth holds you steady.

advanced.name: Season's Turning
advanced.description: Once per scene, you may shift your fighting style to match the current season. Spring: +1 die to healing and recovery actions; Summer: +1 die to strength and endurance; Autumn: +1 die to perception and stealth; Winter: +1 die to defense and resistance. This benefit lasts for the scene.

master.name: The Unmoving Oak
master.description: Once per session, you may become immovable for one exchange. You cannot be knocked prone, pushed, or moved against your will. Additionally, you gain +2 Armor and may make a free counter-attack against any creature that attacks you in melee.

corruption.benefit: +1 die to Survival and Nature rolls in forested terrain.
corruption.cost: You feel uncomfortable in open spaces without trees; -1 die to rolls in plains or deserts.

corruption.benefit: Once per scene, you may speak with plants and trees as if they were people.
corruption.cost: You begin to prefer the company of trees to people; -1 die to social rolls in cities.

corruption.benefit: +2 dice to resist fear or intimidation when in natural terrain.
corruption.cost: You cannot sleep indoors without suffering 1 Fatigue the next day.

corruption.benefit: Once per session, you may command a single plant or tree to move or attack as if it were an ally (Cap 3).
corruption.cost: You are compelled to defend any wild place you encounter; hesitation costs 1 SB.

corruption.benefit: You can sense the health and mood of any forest or grove within a mile.
corruption.cost: You feel pain when the forest is wounded; when a tree is cut within a mile, mark 1 Fatigue.

corruption.benefit: Once per session, you may become the forest itself—your body dissolves into leaves and roots, gaining immunity to physical damage for one scene.
corruption.cost: Mark +3 Obligation. You can no longer eat cultivated food—only what you hunt or gather yourself. Your skin takes on a bark-like texture.

corruption.benefit: Seasonal Sense: +1 die to predict weather, seasonal shifts, or natural events.
corruption.cost: Cyclical Mood: –1 die to actions that defy the season (haste in winter, patience in spring).

corruption.benefit: Verdant Whisper: Once/scene, gain +2 dice when communing with nature.
corruption.cost: Plant Speech: Under stress, you address plants before people; –1 die to civilized social rolls.

corruption.benefit: Growth's Touch: Once/session, accelerate natural healing or growth.
corruption.cost: Seasonal Shift: Demeanor changes with the season; allies note unsettling variance.

corruption.benefit: Boundary Keeper: Once/scene, sense violations of wild places at Far.
corruption.cost: Wild Intolerance: –1 die in dense urban/cultivated zones; physical discomfort in worked stone.

corruption.benefit: Cycle's Memory: Once/session, perfectly recall a natural event witnessed here.
corruption.cost: Ecosystem Dependency: Without daily time in nature, suffer Fatigue 1.

corruption.benefit: Avatar of Seasons: Once/session, embody a season fully (+3 dice to seasonal actions).
corruption.cost: Nature's Claim: Mark +2 Obligation; risk becoming bound to a specific biome. You may no longer eat cultivated food—only what you hunt, gather, or grow yourself.

playstyle_notes.description: Grimmir rewards those who approach the wild with fear and respect, not dominion. His followers are not masters of nature but participants in its rituals—they know when to give blood, when to leave an offering, and when to simply bow and walk away. Intrusions often take the form of seasonal demands: a grove that must be fed before the first frost, a creature that must be hunted before it hunts you, or a vision of a ritual that must be performed at the next solstice. Refusal does not invite wrath—merely the withdrawal of the wild's protection, leaving the follower exposed to the very fears they once understood. Ideal for druids, rangers, and characters who understand that the forest is not a resource but a creditor.
emphasizes: Seasonal Sacrifice: the old ways of blood and offering
Folk Horror: the terror of the unseen and the ritual that must be performed
Primal Mystery: knowledge hidden in root and stone, omens and portents
Growth from Death: decay as the engine of new life
Boundary Keeping: guarding the threshold between the civilized and the wild

sample_adventure.title: The Root-Moot's Reckoning
sample_adventure.description: A village's harvest fails for the third year in a row. The elders whisper of a broken boundary—a stone marker was moved to expand a field, and the forest has turned hostile. The Root-Moot sends a messenger to the party: 'The Old Man is hungry. The field must be returned to the wild, or the wild will take the village instead.'
sample_adventure.quote: The root does not bargain. It grows, or it rots. The choice is yours, but the season does not wait.

guises.name: The Alder King
guises.note: A household leaves the oldest tree out of its account of what may be cut. The wood around it can be worked, argued over, and inherited; the tree is addressed differently. A newcomer who asks which lord owns it may receive a useful answer about every other tree on the slope. Nobody supplies a genealogy to make that answer easier.

guises.name: The Thorn-Father
guises.note: His sign is allowed to grow crooked. Hedge-cutting gathers neighbors who disagree about nearly everything except where the work must stop. A gap is not improved merely because a cart would pass more easily through it. When something stands beyond the hedge after dusk, the household continues the meal without asking it to identify itself.

guises.name: The Root-Father
guises.note: Small shrines stand among fungus and lichen where the living growth reaches stone. Aelerian keepers honor persistence under a sheltered slope; Tavarun households attend to roots pressing into wet masonry. Their observances answer different mountains. They do not identify every root that enters an undervault as a message from one king.

guises.name: The Sky-Wolf
guises.note: The figure follows the herds rather than a forest boundary. Hunts remember where game returned after a hard season and where it did not. This name links Grimmir to the movement of living country; it does not make him Kuva or assign him sovereignty over every steppe spirit. A hunter may honor both without placing either in the other's household.

guises.name: The Keeper Outside the Wall
guises.note: Estate sanctuaries place a rough branch beside polished agricultural images. Learned owners compare the figure to several ancient rustic powers; workers know which strip was left uncut before the estate acquired a name. A patron's description of picturesque wilderness can be younger than the household whose work has kept it there.

provenance.origin: His cults remember boundaries and encounters more readily than a first foundation.
provenance.summary: The Root-Moot preserves a tradition of masked gatherings beneath old trees. Its songs change with the country and often refuse a sequence that would turn them into a king's life. Some singers say Grimmir was waiting when their people arrived. Others say he has always belonged to the place and find the distinction unnecessary. A temple catalogue that gives him one birthplace has obtained a neater answer than the keepers provide.
provenance.the_migration: Migrants took a branch, a mask, or a season's refrain into new country. The observance did not always settle there unchanged. An Aeler household finding roots beneath a new threshold could recognize the Root-Father without possessing its neighbor's Thorn-Father custom. Hunters on the steppe translated a figure encountered at the forest edge into the Sky-Wolf following the herds. These recognitions are not proof that every landscape has agreed to the same terms.
provenance.why_it_took: Landholders adopted the cult where an older boundary constrained a claim. Some observed it faithfully. Others offered an impressive new sanctuary while clearing the place people had actually avoided. The quarrel is not always between ignorant laborers and an enlightened protector of nature: a family may need fuel, a proprietor may need a boundary moved, and the thing in the uncut ground has not explained its interest to either.
provenance.note: Keep Grimmir distinct from local spirits, the Ukwe's powers, and the Couatl. A shared concern with living country does not reduce Sekogo or every forest people to worshippers of the Alder King. Nor does a rural title turn him into a safe agricultural benefactor.

philosophy.name: What the Clearing Leaves Outside
philosophy.summary: Grimmir's followers live by taking from country that has other inhabitants. Respect is not a guarantee that the taking will be permitted.
philosophy.the_point: It is tempting to turn him into the spokesman for whatever management plan seems best. That gives a human argument an authority the Patron has not supplied. A careful forester may still meet something their careful practice cannot placate.
philosophy.the_third_thing: The useful humility is to acknowledge a limit without pretending to understand all of it. A boundary can be observed for generations while its keeper remains unable to explain what stands on the other side.
philosophy.at_the_table: Put a needed resource across an old limit. Establish observable warnings and consequences, but do not require a speech in which the Alder King explains the correct policy. Negotiating with the people affected should remain meaningful even when the supernatural question remains open.
